claim: Mammalian two-pore-channels (TPC1, 2; TPCN1, TPCN2) are ubiquitously-expressed, PI(3,5)P2-activated, Na+-selective channels in the endosomes and lysosomes.
source: Mammalian two-pore-channels (TPC1, 2; TPCN1, TPCN2) are ubiquitously- expressed, PI(3,5)P2-activated, Na+-selective channels in the endosomes and lysosomes that regulate luminal pH homeostasis, membrane trafficking, and Ebola viral infection.
evidence: This is a well-established characterization of TPC channels supported by prior research and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: TPC channels regulate luminal pH homeostasis, membrane trafficking, and Ebola viral infection.
source: Mammalian two-pore-channels (TPC1, 2; TPCN1, TPCN2) are ubiquitously- expressed, PI(3,5)P2-activated, Na+-selective channels in the endosomes and lysosomes that regulate luminal pH homeostasis, membrane trafficking, and Ebola viral infection.
evidence: These functional roles are stated as established knowledge about TPC channels.

claim: The channel activity of TPC1 is strongly dependent on membrane voltage.
source: Whereas the channel activity of TPC1 is strongly dependent on membrane voltage, TPC2 lacks such voltage dependence despite the presence of the presumed 'S4 voltage-sensing' domains.
evidence: This is stated as an established characteristic of TPC1 and is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: TPC2 lacks voltage dependence despite the presence of the presumed 'S4 voltage-sensing' domains.
source: Whereas the channel activity of TPC1 is strongly dependent on membrane voltage, TPC2 lacks such voltage dependence despite the presence of the presumed 'S4 voltage-sensing' domains.
evidence: This is stated as an established characteristic of TPC2 and is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Tricyclic anti-depressants (TCAs) are small-molecule agonists of TPC channels.
source: By performing high-throughput screening followed by lysosomal electrophysiology, here we identified a class of tricyclic anti-depressants (TCAs) as small-molecule agonists of TPC channels.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by extensive electrophysiological data in Figures 1-3.

claim: TCAs activate both TPC1 and TPC2 in a voltage-dependent manner.
source: TCAs activate both TPC1 and TPC2 in a voltage-dependent manner, referred to as Lysosomal Na+ channel Voltage-dependent Activators (LyNa-VAs).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: TCAs are referred to as Lysosomal Na+ channel Voltage-dependent Activators (LyNa-VAs).
source: TCAs activate both TPC1 and TPC2 in a voltage-dependent manner, referred to as Lysosomal Na+ channel Voltage-dependent Activators (LyNa-VAs).
evidence: This is the nomenclature introduced by the authors for TCAs that activate TPC channels.

claim: Another compound (Riluzole/LyNA1) activates TPC2 independent of voltage, like PI(3,5)P2.
source: We also identified another compound which, like PI(3,5)P2, activates TPC2 independent of voltage, suggesting the existence of agonist-specific gating mechanisms.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 1H and Figure 2D.

claim: Agonist-specific gating mechanisms exist in TPC channels.
source: We also identified another compound which, like PI(3,5)P2, activates TPC2 independent of voltage, suggesting the existence of agonist-specific gating mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential voltage-dependence observed with different agonists (TCAs vs. PI(3,5)P2 vs. LyNA1).

claim: Small-molecule TPC agonists can facilitate studies of the cell biological roles of TPCs.
source: Our identification of small-molecule TPC agonists should facilitate the studies of the cell biological roles of TPCs and can also readily explain the reported effects of TCAs in the modulation of autophagy and lysosomal functions.
evidence: This is a prospective statement about the utility of the identified compounds.

claim: The identified TPC agonists can explain the reported effects of TCAs in the modulation of autophagy and lysosomal functions.
source: Our identification of small-molecule TPC agonists should facilitate the studies of the cell biological roles of TPCs and can also readily explain the reported effects of TCAs in the modulation of autophagy and lysosomal functions.
evidence: This is a speculative connection between the findings and previously reported TCA effects.

claim: Patch-clamp studies of isolated lysosomal membranes have discovered multiple lysosomal channels that are selective for Na+, K+, Ca2+, and Cl-.
source: Patch-clamp studies of isolated lysosomal membranes have recently discovered multiple lysosomal channels that are selective for Na+, K+, Ca2+, and Cl- (Cang et al., 2015; Cang et al., 2013; Cao et al., 2015; Dong et al., 2010; Li et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2012; Xiong and Zhu, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Small-molecule synthetic agonists of Mucolipin TRP channels (ML-SAs) have been instrumental in revealing the functions of these Ca2+ release channels in lysosomal exocytosis, mobility, and biogenesis.
source: For example, small-molecule synthetic agonists of Mucolipin TRP channels (TRPMLs), that is ML-SAs, have been instrumental in revealing the functions of these Ca2+ release channels in lysosomal exocytosis, mobility, and biogenesis (Li et al., 2016; Shen et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research demonstrating the utility of ML-SAs.

claim: TPC proteins are ubiquitously expressed, dimeric, two-repeat (2 × 6 TM) cation channels localized exclusively in the intracellular endosomes and lysosomes.
source: Two-pore channel proteins (TPC1, 2; TPCN1, TPCN2) are ubiquitously expressed, dimeric, two-repeat (2 × 6 TM) cation channels that are localized exclusively in the intracellular endosomes and lysosomes (Calcraft et al., 2009; Grimm et al., 2017; Morgan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a structural and localization characterization supported by citations.

claim: TPCs regulate organellar membrane excitability, membrane trafficking, and pH homeostasis at the cellular level.
source: At the cellular level, TPCs regulate organellar membrane excitability, membrane trafficking, and pH homeostasis; at the organismal level, TPCs regulate various physiological and pathological processes, including hair pigmentation, Ebola viral infection, and cancer growth (Ambrosio et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2017; Sakurai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TPCs regulate hair pigmentation, Ebola viral infection, and cancer growth at the organismal level.
source: At the cellular level, TPCs regulate organellar membrane excitability, membrane trafficking, and pH homeostasis; at the organismal level, TPCs regulate various physiological and pathological processes, including hair pigmentation, Ebola viral infection, and cancer growth (Ambrosio et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2017; Sakurai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: It remains controversial whether TPCs are the bona fide NAADP receptor.
source: However, it remains controversial whether TPCs are the bona fide NAADP receptor (Lin-Moshier et al., 2012; Morgan et al., 2015; Walseth et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to conflicting research findings.

claim: Several recent endolysosomal patch-clamp studies have demonstrated that TPCs are Na+-selective channels activated by PI(3,5)P2.
source: Indeed, several recent endolysosomal patch-clamp studies have demonstrated that TPCs are Na+-selective channels activated by PI(3,5)P2 (Bellono et al., 2016; Cang et al., 2014; Cang et al., 2013; Guo et al., 2017; Jha et al., 2014; Kirsch et al., 2018; She et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2012), a late endosome and lysosome-specific phosphoinositide that is known to regulate many aspects of lysosome function (McCartney et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent patch-clamp studies.

claim: PI(3,5)P2 is a late endosome and lysosome-specific phosphoinositide that regulates many aspects of lysosome function.
source: Indeed, several recent endolysosomal patch-clamp studies have demonstrated that TPCs are Na+-selective channels activated by PI(3,5)P2 (Bellono et al., 2016; Cang et al., 2014; Cang et al., 2013; Guo et al., 2017; Jha et al., 2014; Kirsch et al., 2018; She et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2012), a late endosome and lysosome-specific phosphoinositide that is known to regulate many aspects of lysosome function (McCartney et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Several amino acid residues in the selectivity filter of TPCs confer the selectivity of Na+ over K+ or Ca2+.
source: Recent high-resolution structural studies revealed that several amino acid (AA) residues in the selectivity filter of TPCs confer the selectivity of Na+ over K+ or Ca2+ (Guo et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2017), and that PI(3,5)P2 binds directly to several positively charged AA residues in the S4-S5 linker to induce channel opening (Kirsch et al., 2018; She et al., 2018; She et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: PI(3,5)P2 binds directly to several positively charged AA residues in the S4-S5 linker to induce channel opening.
source: Recent high-resolution structural studies revealed that several amino acid (AA) residues in the selectivity filter of TPCs confer the selectivity of Na+ over K+ or Ca2+ (Guo et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2017), and that PI(3,5)P2 binds directly to several positively charged AA residues in the S4-S5 linker to induce channel opening (Kirsch et al., 2018; She et al., 2018; She et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Direct activation of TPCs by sphingosines was not confirmed in lysosomal electrophysiological assays.
source: Sphingosines also reportedly induce TPC1-mediated Ca2+ release from the lysosomes (Höglinger et al., 2015), but direct activation of TPCs by sphingosines was not confirmed in the lysosomal electrophysiological assays (unpublished data in the Xu laboratory) (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on unpublished data from the authors' laboratory.

claim: TPCs contain multiple positively-charged AA residues in their voltage sensor domains (S4), which are believed to confer voltage-dependent activation of plant and animal TPC1 channels.
source: Like canonical voltage-gated cation channels, TPCs contain multiple positively-charged AA residues in their voltage sensor domains (S4), which are believed to confer voltage-dependent activation of plant and animal TPC1 channels (Cang et al., 2014; She et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TPC2 activation is completely voltage-independent, despite the presence of multiple Arginine/Lysine residues in their S4 helices.
source: In a sharp contrast, TPC2 activation is completely voltage-independent, despite the presence of multiple Arginine/Lysine residues in their S4 helices (Cang et al., 2014; Cang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: 23 compounds from the LOPAC library induced Ca2+ increases in TPC2 stable cells.
source: Among the positive hits, 23 compounds induced Ca2+ increases in TPC2 stable cells (Figure 1A and B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), but not in cells stably expressing TRPML14A (a surface-expressing mutant TRPML1 [Shen et al., 2012]) channels (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The 23 compounds that induced Ca2+ increases in TPC2 stable cells did not induce Ca2+ increases in cells stably expressing TRPML14A channels.
source: Among the positive hits, 23 compounds induced Ca2+ increases in TPC2 stable cells (Figure 1A and B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), but not in cells stably expressing TRPML14A (a surface-expressing mutant TRPML1 [Shen et al., 2012]) channels (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as a negative result to demonstrate specificity.

claim: 5 out of the 23 compounds are well characterized as tri-cyclic anti-depressants (TCAs).
source: To our surprise, 5 out of the 23 compounds are well characterized as tri-cyclic anti-depressants (TCAs), which are believed to act on neurotransmitter transporters or voltage-gated Na+ channels (Cheng and Bahar, 2019; Pancrazio et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on TCAs.

claim: TCAs are believed to act on neurotransmitter transporters or voltage-gated Na+ channels.
source: To our surprise, 5 out of the 23 compounds are well characterized as tri-cyclic anti-depressants (TCAs), which are believed to act on neurotransmitter transporters or voltage-gated Na+ channels (Cheng and Bahar, 2019; Pancrazio et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on TCAs.

claim: All five TCAs robustly and rapidly activated whole-cell currents in TPC2LL/AA-expressing cells.
source: All five TCAs robustly and rapidly activated whole-cell currents in TPC2LL/AA-expressing cells (Wang et al., 2012), but not in non-transfected HEK293 cells (Figure 1C and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D, Table 1, and Table 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: TCAs did not activate whole-cell currents in non-transfected HEK293 cells.
source: All five TCAs robustly and rapidly activated whole-cell currents in TPC2LL/AA-expressing cells (Wang et al., 2012), but not in non-transfected HEK293 cells (Figure 1C and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D, Table 1, and Table 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a negative control demonstrating specificity of TCA effects to TPC2-expressing cells.

claim: Clomipramine activated whole-cell TPC2LL/AA-mediated strongly rectifying currents with an EC50 of 43 ± 2 μM.
source: Of them, Clomipramine activated whole-cell TPC2LL/AA-mediated strongly rectifying currents (ITPC2-LL/AA) with an EC50 of 43 ± 2 μM (n = 4 patches) (Figure 1D and E, and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1E and Table 1.

claim: Chlorpromazine had an EC50 of 60 ± 2 μM for TPC2 activation.
source: Another structurally different TCA, Chlorpromazine, had an EC50 of 60 ± 2 μM (n = 4 patches), and was referred to as LyNa-VA2.1 (Figure 1E, Table 1, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1E and Table 1.

claim: All TCA-induced currents exhibited strong voltage-dependence and inward rectification.
source: All TCA-induced currents exhibited strong voltage-dependence and inward rectification, which resembled TRPML1-mediated currents (ITRPML1) (Shen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: None of the TCAs had any activation effect on ITRPML1.
source: However, none of the TCAs had any activation effect on ITRPML1 (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1F and G demonstrating specificity.

claim: Riluzole is an FDA-approved amyotrophic lateral sclerosis drug that is known to modulate voltage-gated Na+ channels.
source: Riluzole, an FDA-approved amyotrophic lateral sclerosis drug that is known to modulate voltage-gated Na+ channels (Liu and Wang, 2018), activated large and linear whole-cell currents in TPC2LL/AA-expressing HEK293 cells (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 3), but not in non-transfected HEK293 cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research on Riluzole.

claim: Riluzole activated large and linear whole-cell currents in TPC2LL/AA-expressing HEK293 cells.
source: Riluzole, an FDA-approved amyotrophic lateral sclerosis drug that is known to modulate voltage-gated Na+ channels (Liu and Wang, 2018), activated large and linear whole-cell currents in TPC2LL/AA-expressing HEK293 cells (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 3), but not in non-transfected HEK293 cells.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Riluzole did not activate currents in non-transfected HEK293 cells.
source: Riluzole, an FDA-approved amyotrophic lateral sclerosis drug that is known to modulate voltage-gated Na+ channels (Liu and Wang, 2018), activated large and linear whole-cell currents in TPC2LL/AA-expressing HEK293 cells (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 3), but not in non-transfected HEK293 cells.
evidence: This is a negative control demonstrating specificity.

claim: More than one agonist-specific gating mechanism (voltage-dependent and voltage-independent) may co-exist within one channel protein.
source: Hence, more than one agonist-specific gating (voltage-dependent and voltage-independent) mechanism may co-exist within one channel protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential voltage-dependence observed with different agonists.

claim: TCAs are lysosomotropic compounds that are known to be highly accumulating in the lysosomes due to proton trapping.
source: TCAs, with a general structure of an aromatic greasy core and an aliphatic chain containing a terminal amine, are lysosomotropic compounds that are known to be highly accumulating in the lysosomes due to proton trapping (Beckmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research on TCA properties.

claim: Both LyNa-VAs and LyNA1 readily activated ITPC2 in TPC2-positive enlarged LELs isolated from transfected Cos1 cells.
source: In TPC2-positive enlarged LELs isolated from transfected Cos1 cells, little or no basal whole-endolysosome currents were seen under symmetric (pipette/luminal and bath/cytosolic) Na+ solutions (Figure 2A). Consistent with our previous studies, bath application of PI(3,5)P2, the endogenous agonist of TPCs (Wang et al., 2012), activated a large whole-endolysosome ITPC2 with linear I-V (Figure 2B and E). Both LyNa-VAs and LyNA1 readily activated ITPC2, although the I-Vs were dramatically different (Figure 2C, D and E, and Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by whole-endolysosome recordings shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: No current activation was seen for LyNa-VAs or LyNA1 in TRPML1-transfected cells.
source: In contrast, no current activation was seen for LyNa-VAs or LyNA1 in TRPML1-transfected cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a negative control demonstrating specificity shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both LyNa-VAs and LyNA1 activated whole-endolysosome ITPC in WT HAP1 cells, but not HAP1 cells lacking TPC1 or TPC2.
source: Both LyNa-VAs and LyNA1 activated whole-endolysosome ITPC in WT HAP1 cells, but not HAP1 cells lacking TPC1 or TPC2 (TPC1−/−/TPC2−/−, TPC1/2 DKO; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the activation effects of both TCAs and LyNA1 on TPCs are specific.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 using knockout cells as negative controls.

claim: The activation effects of both TCAs and LyNA1 on TPCs are specific.
source: Both LyNa-VAs and LyNA1 activated whole-endolysosome ITPC in WT HAP1 cells, but not HAP1 cells lacking TPC1 or TPC2 (TPC1−/−/TPC2−/−, TPC1/2 DKO; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the activation effects of both TCAs and LyNA1 on TPCs are specific.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of activation in TPC1/2 DKO cells.

claim: LyNa-VAs and LyNA1 are likely to be membrane permeable, activating TPC2 via direct agonist binding.
source: In addition, robust activation of ITPC2 in the whole-cell configuration with agonists being applied from the extracellular side (analogous to the luminal side in the lysosome), as well as in the inside-out (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) and whole-endolysosome configurations with agonists being applied from the cytosolic side, suggests that LyNa-VAs and LyNA1 are likely to be membrane permeable, activating TPC2 via direct agonist binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the ability of agonists to activate channels when applied from different sides of the membrane.

claim: The action site of LyNa-VAs is likely to be either intracellular or more accessible from the intracellular side.
source: As the channel activation in the whole-cell recordings was significantly slower, that is longer latency and time course of activation, compared to the inside-out and whole-endolysosome recordings (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2), the action site of LyNa-VAs is likely to be either intracellular or more accessible from the intracellular side.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic differences in activation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: TPC2 currents activated by TCAs were strongly voltage-dependent in both whole-cell and whole-endolysosome recordings.
source: In contrast, TPC2 currents activated by TCAs were strongly voltage-dependent, in both whole-cell and whole-endolysosome recordings, no matter whether the currents were elicited by a voltage ramp or a series of voltage steps (see Figure 2C and E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2C and E.

claim: TCA-activated step currents displayed prominent inactivation and strong inward rectification.
source: In both whole-cell and whole-endolysosome configurations, TCA-activated step currents displayed prominent inactivation and strong inward rectification (Figure 2C, E and F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting the existence of voltage-dependent activation and/or inactivation gating processes.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2C, E and F.

claim: LyNa-VA-activated ITPC2 exhibited substantial time-dependent inactivation at negative voltages.
source: Under the voltage-step protocols, LyNa-VA-activated ITPC2 exhibited substantial time-dependent inactivation at negative voltages (Figure 2C and G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2C and G.

claim: The activation by LyNa-VA1.2 was strongly dependent on voltage, with a half-maximal activation voltage (V1/2) of −20 mV at the concentration of 100 μM.
source: When we used a tail-current protocol to study the voltage-dependent activation, the activation by LyNa-VA1.2 was strongly dependent on voltage, with a half-maximal activation voltage (V1/2) of −20 mV at the concentration of 100 μM (Figure 2J and K).
evidence: This is supported by tail-current analysis shown in Figure 2J and K.

claim: No apparent voltage-dependent activation was seen when whole-endolysosome ITPC2 was activated by PI(3,5)P2 or LyNA1.
source: In contrast, no apparent voltage-dependent activation was seen when whole-endolysosome ITPC2 was activated by PI(3,5)P2 (Figure 2I and K) or LyNA1.
evidence: This is supported by tail-current analysis shown in Figure 2I and K.

claim: PI(3,5)P2 reportedly binds to Lys204 and adjacent AA residues to activate TPC2.
source: PI(3,5)P2 reportedly binds to Lys204 and adjacent AA residues to activate TPC2 (She et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior structural research.

claim: LyNa-VA and LyNA1 still robustly activated whole-endolysosome ITPC2 in cells transfected with a PI(3,5)P2-insensitive mutant TPC2 channel (K204A).
source: In the cells that were transfected with a PI(3,5)P2-insensitive mutant TPC2 channel (K204A) (She et al., 2019), LyNa-VA and LyNA1 still robustly activated whole-endolysosome ITPC2 (Figure 3A and B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Much dramatic LyNa-VA activation was seen in the presence of a low concentration of PI(3,5)P2 (50 nM).
source: Much dramatic LyNa-VA activation was seen in the presence of a low concentration of PI(3,5)P2 (50 nM; Figure 3C and D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), and this synergism was nearly abolished in TPC2K204A mutant channels (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and D demonstrating synergistic effects.

claim: The synergism between LyNa-VA and PI(3,5)P2 was nearly abolished in TPC2K204A mutant channels.
source: Much dramatic LyNa-VA activation was seen in the presence of a low concentration of PI(3,5)P2 (50 nM; Figure 3C and D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), and this synergism was nearly abolished in TPC2K204A mutant channels (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: An additive but not synergistic activation was observed between LyNA1 and PI(3,5)P2.
source: In contrast, an additive but not synergistic activation was observed between LyNA1 and PI(3,5)P2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: LyNa-VAs activated or modulated TPC2 via a unique, PI(3,5)P2-independent but voltage-dependent mechanism.
source: Collectively, these results suggested that LyNa-VAs activated or modulated TPC2 via a unique, PI(3,5)P2-independent but voltage-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the ability of LyNa-VAs to activate the K204A mutant and the synergistic effects with PI(3,5)P2.

claim: TPC1 shows substantial voltage-dependent currents in the absence of any exogenous agonist.
source: In contrast to TPC2, which produces little or no current at any potential under basal conditions, yet a large, voltage-independent conductance increases in the presence of PI(3,5)P2, TPC1 shows substantial voltage-dependent currents in the absence of any exogenous agonist (Cang et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: LyNa-VA1.1 produced a profound suppression of outward currents at potentials positive to Erev and a substantial enhancement of inward currents negative to Erev in TPC1.
source: First, when membrane voltage was stepped to various test potentials after a prolonged pre-pulse to +80 mV and the currents were compared to the basal currents, LyNa-VA1.1 produced a profound suppression of outward currents at potentials positive to Erev (~0 mV), and a substantial enhancement of inward currents negative to Erev (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Upon LyNa-VA1 activation, the I-V of TPC1 completely reversed from strong outward rectification to strong inward rectification.
source: Hence, upon LyNa-VA1 activation, the I-V of TPC1 completely reversed from strong outward rectification to strong inward rectification (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by I-V plots shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Both LyNa-VA2.1 and LyNA1 inhibited ITPC1.
source: Intriguingly, unlike LyNa-VA1.1 and LyNa-VA1.2, which activated inward ITPC2 with EC50s within micromolar ranges, both LyNa-VA2.1 and LyNA1 inhibited ITPC1 (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The effect of LyNa-VA1.1 was to shift the midpoint of activation voltage (V1/2) by −65 mV as compared to the basal condition in TPC1.
source: The effect of LyNa-VA1.1 was to shift the midpoint of activation voltage (V1/2) by −65 mV as compared to the basal condition, and to slow down the deactivation time course (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: This is supported by tail-current analysis shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: LyNa-VA1.1 slowed down the deactivation time course of TPC1.
source: The effect of LyNa-VA1.1 was to shift the midpoint of activation voltage (V1/2) by −65 mV as compared to the basal condition, and to slow down the deactivation time course (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: This is supported by tail-current analysis shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: The R540I mutation was reported to abolish TPC1 activation by membrane depolarization.
source: It was recently reported that the R540I mutation, which removes a positive charge in the second putative voltage-sensing 'S4-type' helix, abolished TPC1 activation by membrane depolarization (She et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In the authors' hands, depolarization still robustly activated voltage-dependent currents in the whole-endolysosomes of hTPC1R540I-expressing cells.
source: However, in our hands, depolarization still robustly activated voltage-dependent currents in the whole-endolysosomes of hTPC1R540I -expressing cells (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4G and H, contradicting prior reports.

claim: LyNa-VA1.1 produced a dramatic enhancement of inward currents at negative potentials in TPC1R540I, indicative of a substantial negative shift in the V1/2 of voltage activation.
source: When LyNa-VA1.1 was tested on endolysosomes overexpressing TPC1R540I, there was also a dramatic enhancement of inward currents at negative potentials indicative of a substantial negative shift in the V1/2 of voltage activation (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: When exposed to PI(3,5)P2, ITPC1 showed a large enhancement at negative potentials indicative of a negative shift in the V1/2 of activation.
source: Finally, when exposed to PI(3,5)P2, ITPC1 showed a large enhancement at negative potentials indicative of a negative shift in the V1/2 of activation, while TPC1R540I -positive endolysosomes showed large currents at all potentials (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B and C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B and C.

claim: TPC1R540I-positive endolysosomes showed large currents at all potentials when exposed to PI(3,5)P2.
source: Finally, when exposed to PI(3,5)P2, ITPC1 showed a large enhancement at negative potentials indicative of a negative shift in the V1/2 of activation, while TPC1R540I -positive endolysosomes showed large currents at all potentials (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B and C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B and C.

claim: The charge-introducing mutation at Ile551 of TPC2 conferred a voltage-dependence to the mutant channel but failed to affect LyNa-VA1.2 activation.
source: The charge-introducing mutation at Ile551 of TPC2 (She et al., 2019), the equivalent site of TPC1R540, conferred a voltage-dependence to the mutant channel but failed to affect LyNa-VA1.2 activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D and E.

claim: The S4 voltage-sensing domains may play a modulatory role, but there exist intrinsic or extrinsic voltage-sensing mechanisms elsewhere responsible for the voltage-dependent gating of TPCs.
source: Put together, these results suggested that whereas the S4 voltage-sensing domains may play a modulatory role, there exist intrinsic or extrinsic voltage-sensing mechanisms elsewhere responsible for the voltage-dependent gating of TPCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutational analyses showing that S4 mutations do not fully explain voltage-dependence.

claim: LyNa-VA1.2- and LyNA1-induced whole-endolysosome ITPC2 was highly selective for Na+ over K+.
source: Like PI(3,5)P2-activated ITPC2 (Figure 5A–C and K), LyNa-VA1.2- and LyNA1-induced whole-endolysosome ITPC2 was highly selective for Na+ over K+, as substitution of bath/cytoplasmic Na+ with K+ significantly shifted Erev to more positive values (Figures 1H, 5D–F and K and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by ion substitution experiments shown in Figure 5D-F and K.

claim: LyNa-VA1.2- and LyNA1-activated ITPC2 exhibited low Ca2+ permeability.
